title: Time exponents for multiple-string LCS over fixed alphabets
formal: Determine the optimal deterministic polynomial-time exponent function \(\tau(\sigma,k)\) for longest common subsequence of \(k\) strings over an alphabet of size \(\sigma\), on the entire domain \(D=\{(\sigma,k)\in\mathbb N^2:\sigma\ge2,\ k\ge2\}\). For each fixed pair, let \[\tau(\sigma,k)=\inf\bigl\{c\ge0:\ \exists A\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \forall(s_1,\ldots,s_k)\in(\{1,\ldots,\sigma\}^{\le n})^k,\ A\text{ outputs an LCS within }Cn^c\text{ operations}\bigr\},\] where \(A\) ranges over the correct uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithms defined below, and \(n,n_0\) are integers. Supply a function \(g:D\to\mathbb R\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|g(\sigma,k)-\tau(\sigma,k)|\le1/100\) for every \((\sigma,k)\in D\). This explicitly broadens the source’s proposed constant-fraction exponent improvement into determination of the underlying exponent function; it is not claimed to be equivalent to that yes/no question.
why: Multiple-string alignment has a rapidly growing dependence on the number of sequences, even though it is polynomial-time solvable when that number is fixed. A small alphabet may constrain the combinatorial choices enough to change the leading exponent. Determining the full exponent function would separate the cost of coordinating many strings from the expressiveness supplied by a growing alphabet, and would sharpen the fine-grained limits behind exact sequence comparison.
status_note: The 2017 source explicitly poses the fixed-alphabet exponent-saving question. This card records a transparent quantitative broadening to the underlying exponent function, not an equivalent reformulation or a claim that every parameter pair is unresolved. Bounded later-work checks through 14 September 2026 found conditional bounds and different string variants, but no unconditional determination of this entire function.

progress.text: Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams, Theorem 2, show that an exponent improvement for k-LCS with alphabet size proportional to k would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. The alphabet dependence is part of the result.

Bringmann poses the fixed-alphabet fractional-exponent improvement in Section 4.3, Open Problem 3, printed page 120. Section 4.2 defines the common-subsequence task and asks a different time-space question.

Golan et al., CPM 2026, review the multiple-string worst-case bounds in Section 1 and obtain algorithms for a hybrid that also imposes a substring requirement. Their result does not determine the exponent function here.

sentences: Multiple-string LCS finds a longest string that occurs as a subsequence of every input.
The target is the optimal deterministic time exponent for every fixed alphabet size and fixed number of strings.
It makes the source’s question about a fractional exponent saving into an explicitly broader quantitative function.
Resolving the function would identify how alphabet size changes the computational cost of coordinating many sequences.
Acceptance requires a Lean-certified error of at most one hundredth at every parameter pair, while retaining the source question separately.

definitions: A subsequence of a string \(s\) is any string obtained by deleting positions while preserving the order of the retained symbols. An LCS of \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) is a string that is a subsequence of every input and has maximum possible length. The algorithm must output one such string exactly, with arbitrary tie-breaking; inputs may have unequal lengths or be empty. The input includes an integer bound \(n\ge2\), the \(k\) lengths and all symbols, stored explicitly in a read-only array with one length or symbol per word; each length is at most \(n\). Output symbols and output length are written explicitly. For each fixed \((\sigma,k)\), the algorithm is one finite program independent of \(n\), with no nonuniform advice or tables supplied as a function of \(n\). Its word width is \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for some fixed integer \(d\ge\sigma+k+4\), allowed to depend on the program and the fixed pair. A constant number of word reads, writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, additions, subtractions, multiplications modulo \(2^W\), or unsigned divisions with quotient and remainder by a nonzero word each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(W\) returns zero. Work memory starts at zero; all input access, preprocessing, addressing and output are charged. Each local operation accesses only constantly many words, and no real arithmetic, oracle, quantum operation or random coins are allowed. Running time is worst-case over all valid tuples for the stated length bound. The constants \(C,n_0,d\) and program may depend on \(\sigma,k\), but not on \(n\) or the input strings. An admissible algorithm must be correct and terminate on every valid input, including sizes below \(n_0\). The alphabet and string count remain fixed when taking the exponent; neither is hidden as a growing function of \(n\). The infimum is finite: exact multiple-string LCS has an \(O(n^k)\) algorithm for each fixed pair, while explicitly outputting a length-\(n\) common string requires linear time. Thus \(1\le\tau(\sigma,k)\le k\). No algorithm attaining the infimum is assumed to exist.
answer_criterion: Provide one unambiguous mathematical function \(g\) on all of \(D\), together with a complete correct proof checked in Lean of the pointwise absolute bound \(1/100\) in exponent units. A family of certified intervals of width at most \(1/50\) covering every pair qualifies through their midpoints. The answer may be an expression or certified evaluation rule; merely repeating the defining infimum is not a determination. Bounds on the infimum must respect its possible nonattainment: a claimed endpoint need not be achieved by one algorithm with exactly that exponent. A result only for one alphabet, one number of strings, average-case inputs, approximations, or substring variants does not meet the entire criterion. Conditional bounds alone do not give an unconditional determination. The tolerance concerns the real-valued exponent function, not an approximation to the output subsequence or a constant-factor characterization of the full running time.

context_blocks.text: Bringmann’s Open Problem 3 asks whether \(k\)-LCS has an \(O(n^{(1-\varepsilon_\Sigma)k})\) algorithm for a fixed alphabet \(\Sigma\). The surrounding paragraph contrasts this with conditional \(n^{k-o(1)}\) hardness when the alphabet can grow linearly with \(k\). Recovering this alphabet dependence is essential; the inherited title alone omitted it.

The benchmark’s permitted quantitative broadening is used here to ask for \(\tau(\sigma,k)\). The original proposed fractional saving remains a separate sourced question. In particular, approximating every exponent to \(1/100\) need not decide whether an arbitrarily small strict exponent improvement exists or whether an infimum is attained. No equivalence between those targets is asserted.

Subsequences retain order while allowing gaps. Requiring a contiguous substring, an increasing sequence, a compressed representation, or a multiplicative approximation changes the task. The unrestricted worst case also differs from parameter bounds that become fast only when the optimum is very close to the input length.

Abboud, Backurs and Vassilevska Williams give conditional exponent lower bounds when the alphabet size is allowed to depend linearly on the number of strings. Their result does not supply the same uniform exponent barrier while one alphabet is held fixed and the number of strings varies. The source also records weaker parameterized hardness for constant alphabets, which leaves room between different linear coefficients in the exponent.

Golan, Kraus, Porat and Shalom review exact multiple-string LCS in CPM 2026 and study a hybrid subsequence–substring requirement. The faster algorithm for that hybrid does not solve unrestricted multiple-string LCS. Their discussion also distinguishes exact algorithms from recent two-string approximation results.
